hook.text: Rats explored a maze for days with no food reward. Then food appeared—and they solved it instantly.

buildup.text: Edward Tolman's 1930s experiment showed the rats had been learning the maze all along, just quietly.

discovery.text: They formed cognitive maps—mental representations of the layout—without any reinforcement.

twist.text: This challenged behaviorism. Learning wasn't just stimulus-response. Internal representations mattered.

climax.text: You do this too. You know your commute layout before you ever need to find a shortcut.

punchline.text: You learn more than you show.

details.summary: Tolman showed that rats who explored a maze without reward learned its layout and demonstrated this knowledge only when later rewarded. Learning can occur without reinforcement or observable behavior change.
details.whyItMatters: Latent learning proved that behavior does not always reflect knowledge. People learn from exploration even without immediate goals, storing information for later use.
takeaways: Learning occurs without reinforcement or visible performance change
Cognitive maps form during unrewarded exploration
Performance emerges only when motivation is present

faq.question: What was Tolman's maze experiment?
faq.answer: Three groups of rats ran a maze. One was always rewarded, one never rewarded, and one rewarded only from day 11. The third group immediately matched the always-rewarded group, showing they had learned the maze layout without reward. The learning was latent until motivation unlocked it.

faq.question: How does latent learning apply to everyday life?
faq.answer: You know the layout of your neighborhood from walking around, not from being rewarded for it. This spatial knowledge emerges when you need to find a new route. Reading widely without a specific purpose builds latent knowledge that surfaces when relevant problems arise later.
